candidate.answerReason: The first square has side 21, giving triangle legs 42 and hypotenuse 42\sqrt2. In the second arrangement, the hypotenuse is divided into three segments each equal to the new square's side, so that side is 14\sqrt2 and its area is 392.

methods.label: Use the 45-degree corner triangles
methods.explanation:
An isosceles right triangle has two \(45^\circ\) angles. The small triangles beside each square therefore have equal legs, which lets us relate the two square sizes.

In Figure \(1\), the square's side is \(\sqrt{441}=21\) cm. Name its upper-left, upper-right, and lower-right vertices \(P,Q,R\), respectively, so \(P\) lies on \(AB\), \(Q\) on \(AC\), and \(R\) on \(BC\). Triangle \(APQ\) is right at \(P\) and has angle \(A=45^\circ\). Its other acute angle is also \(45^\circ\), so \(AP=PQ=21\). Hence
\[
AB=AP+PB=21+21=42.
\]
Since \(AB=BC\), the Pythagorean theorem gives
\[
AC=\sqrt{42^2+42^2}=42\sqrt2.
\]
In Figure \(2\), name the square's vertices \(E,F,G,H\) in order, with \(E\) on \(AB\), \(F,G\) on \(AC\), and \(H\) on \(BC\). Let its side length be \(t>0\). Because adjacent square sides are perpendicular, triangle \(AEF\) is right at \(F\). Its angle at \(A\) is \(45^\circ\), so its legs satisfy \(AF=EF=t\). Similarly, triangle \(CGH\) is right at \(G\) with angle \(C=45^\circ\), giving \(CG=GH=t\).

The three consecutive segments of \(AC\) are therefore
\[
AF=t,\qquad FG=t,\qquad GC=t.
\]
Thus \(3t=42\sqrt2\), so \(t=14\sqrt2\). The second square's area is
\[
t^2=(14\sqrt2)^2=\boxed{392\text{ cm}^2},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
methods.levelReason: The argument uses square properties, equal angles giving equal sides, and the Pythagorean theorem.

methods.label: Compare parallel cross-sections of the triangle
methods.explanation:
A segment parallel to a triangle's base forms a smaller similar triangle. This relates the second square's side to its distance from the hypotenuse.

In Figure \(1\), the square has side \(\sqrt{441}=21\) cm. Let the equal triangle legs have length \(L\). Name the square's upper-left and upper-right vertices \(P\) and \(Q\), with \(P\) on \(AB\) and \(Q\) on \(AC\). Since \(PQ\parallel BC\), triangles \(APQ\) and \(ABC\) are similar. Their corresponding legs give
\[
\frac{L-21}{L}=\frac{21}{L}.
\]
Here \(L>0\), so \(L-21=21\) and \(L=42\). The hypotenuse length is consequently \(b=42\sqrt2\). Let \(h\) be the altitude from \(B\) to \(AC\). In an isosceles triangle this altitude bisects the base, so the Pythagorean theorem gives
\[
h=\sqrt{42^2-(21\sqrt2)^2}=21\sqrt2.
\]
In Figure \(2\), let the square's side be \(t\). One side lies on \(AC\), and the opposite side joins the two legs parallel to \(AC\). The perpendicular separation of those square sides is \(t\). Therefore the smaller triangle at \(B\) has base \(t\) and altitude \(h-t\), where \(0<t<h\).

This smaller triangle is similar to \(ABC\), so corresponding bases and altitudes satisfy
\[
\frac{t}{b}=\frac{h-t}{h}.
\]
Since \(b=2h\) and \(h>0\), this becomes \(t=2(h-t)\). Thus
\[
t=\frac{2h}{3}=14\sqrt2.
\]
This value satisfies \(0<t<h\), as required. The square's area is
\[
t^2=(14\sqrt2)^2=\boxed{392\text{ cm}^2},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
